Boston housing in brief

Boston is the state capital and the seat of Suffolk County. The 2020 census counted 675,647 residents, the most of any city in Massachusetts. A good share of the land came from fill, and Back Bay is one of the areas built on gravel hauled in by train, so soil, basements and foundations differ a lot from one block to the next.

The city recognizes 23 neighborhoods, including Allston, Back Bay, Beacon Hill, Charlestown, Dorchester, East Boston, Fenway, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, Roslindale, Roxbury, South Boston, the South End and West Roxbury. Each can have a different mix of triple-deckers, rowhouses, condos and single families, and all are billed through the same city tax system.

Winters are cold and stormy, so roofs, gutters, heating systems and pipes take the most wear. The median home was built in 1947, which means many houses are due for roof, wiring or boiler work. Waterfront and low-lying streets deserve a closer look at basement moisture. If the repairs are more than you want to take on, selling as-is is one way out, since a cash buyer prices the condition in and you skip the contractor visits.

Who bills and collects Boston property tax

Two offices share the work: Assessing sets the value and Tax Collection sends and collects the bill. Both sit in City Hall at 1 City Hall Square. Assessing is in Room 301, and the Collector is at Window M-30.

Boston runs on a July 1 to June 30 fiscal year and bills quarterly. The first and second quarter bills are estimates built from last year's value and rate. The real rate shows up on the third quarter bill, typically issued in late December.

The 2026 rate is $12.40 per $1,000 for residential property and $26.96 for commercial, industrial and personal property, because Boston classifies property and charges the two classes different rates. Proposition 2½, passed by voters in 1980, caps how fast the city's total levy can grow, but it does not limit growth in an individual assessment.

Tax detailBoston figure

Residential rate, 2026$12.40 per $1,000
Commercial, industrial, personal property$26.96 per $1,000

How the residential exemption works

The residential exemption takes part of a home's value out of taxation if you own it and live in it as your primary residence. It saved qualified homeowners up to $4,353.74 last fiscal year, and the credit is applied to the third quarter bill in late December.

For FY2027 the application is due by April 1, 2027. A recent home rule petition widened the rules: owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and moved in between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may now qualify for the current year. Owners who owned and occupied on January 1, 2026 still qualify.

  • You can claim the exemption on one property only.
  • Filing does not postpone a payment that is due.
  • Other exemptions can stack with it, but taxable value cannot drop below 10 percent of assessed value, with exceptions for some residents with physical ailments or financial hardship.
  • Applications are downloaded from the Boston Property Lookup tool after the December bills go out.

A buyer who moves in can apply for the exemption, so do not promise a buyer a tax figure. Send them to the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center to see what the current bill looks like.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How do I challenge my Boston assessment?

File an abatement application with the Assessing Department by mail or in person before February 1, 2027 for FY2027. Assessing's direct line is 617-635-4288. If the department denies the request, you have three months from its decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board at 100 Cambridge Street, 2nd Floor, Suite 200, Boston, MA 02114, phone 617-727-3100.

Ask the Collector how an open abatement affects the bill you currently owe.

If you own a condo with a deeded parking space, check for two bills. A condo unit appears as class CD and the parking space as class CP, and both must be paid because together they equal the full property value.

What does selling a Boston house involve?

In Massachusetts a house sale is a recorded transaction, and a real estate attorney is normally part of it. Attorneys handle buying and selling by law and by practice, and the deed to 80 to 90 percent of properties is filed as recorded land at the county Registry of Deeds. For Boston that means the Suffolk County registry.

Three state rules show up for most sellers:

  • Deeds excise. The deeds tax is $2.28 per $500 of the sales price, less any mortgage assumed.
  • Smoke and CO certificate. A seller needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the alarms meet requirements for a sale. The fire department charges a fee.
  • Inspection waivers. State regulation 760 CMR 74 says sellers of certain residential properties will not condition an offer on a waiver of the home inspection.

A cash sale keeps all three in place. What changes is who is waiting on repairs and financing.

What to gather before you list

Boston sellers lose time when the paperwork shows up late, so collect it first.

  • Your latest quarterly tax bill and proof of payment for each quarter so far.
  • Any abatement application or Appellate Tax Board filing, with the decision letter if you have one.
  • For a condo, both the unit bill (class CD) and the parking space bill (class CP).
  • Proof of the residential exemption you have been receiving, so your attorney can explain to the buyer that it will not carry over.
  • Your deed and mortgage payoff information, since the deed goes to the Suffolk County registry at closing.

Call the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center at 617-635-4287 with questions about the current year. Because the first two quarterly bills are estimates and the true rate arrives with the third, the amount that has to be split between you and the buyer can shift late in the year, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will handle it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with unpaid property tax

Unpaid tax can be settled from the sale proceeds at closing, which lowers what you take home. Get the exact amount owed from the city before you sign. For current-year questions call 617-635-4287, and for earlier years call the Collector at 617-635-4131.

If the property came to you through probate, tax questions can run alongside other deadlines. Our pages on the Massachusetts estate tax, capital gains and homestead protection cover those separately.

A workable order is to request the payoff, confirm any open abatement with the Collector, line up the fire department certificate, then give your attorney the figures so the closing statement is right the first time.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Boston residential property tax rate?

The 2026 residential rate is $12.40 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial, industrial and personal property rate is $26.96 per $1,000. The final rate for a fiscal year appears on the third quarter bill.

When are Boston property tax abatement applications due?

For fiscal year 2027, the deadline is February 1, 2027. You file with the Assessing Department by mail or in person. If it is denied, you have three months from the decision to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Can I get Boston's residential exemption if I just bought my home?

Possibly. Owners who recorded a deed at the Suffolk County Registry of Deeds and occupied the home between January 1 and June 30, 2026 may qualify for FY2027. The application is due April 1, 2027.

Do I have to pay tax on a condo parking space in Boston?

Yes, if you receive a separate bill. The unit is class CD and the parking space is class CP, and both bills must be paid because together they make up the full property value.

Can I sell a Boston house with unpaid property tax?

Yes, in general. The unpaid amount can be settled from the proceeds at closing. Call the Taxpayer Referral and Assistance Center at 617-635-4287 for the exact amount owed.

Worcester and its Assessing Division

Worcester is the main city of Central Massachusetts, about 40 miles west of Boston, and the seat of Worcester County. It had an estimated 213,862 residents in 2025, second in the state. Many of its houses are 19th-century triple-deckers, so rent and condition affect value. The city's Assessing Division values every parcel for tax.

DetailWorcester Assessing
OfficeCity Hall Room 209, 455 Main Street, Worcester, MA 01608
Phone and email508-799-1098, assessing@worcesterma.gov
HoursMonday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Fiscal yearJuly 1 to June 30
Valuation dateJanuary 1 before the fiscal year
Property classesResidential, Open Space, Commercial, Industrial

Bill dates

Bills go out four times a year, on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1, and each payment falls due 30 days after it is issued.

  • The July 1 and October 1 bills are preliminary, each equal to last year's tax divided by four.
  • The January 1 and April 1 bills are actual. They use the new assessment and rate, subtract the preliminary tax already billed, and split the rest between the two payments.
  • A change in your tax from reassessment therefore shows up only in the third and fourth quarters.

Posted rates are $13.28 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $29.06 per $1,000 for commercial. No fiscal year is attached to them, so check the year printed on your bill before relying on either figure.

How Worcester values a house

Massachusetts requires every city to assess property at full and fair cash value, and the Department of Revenue certifies Worcester's assessments after checking market sales and running valuation audits.

The city's process has three steps. The Assessor values all taxable property, classifies each parcel by use, and then applies the value and class to set the tax. January 1 is the tax date, so what you own and its condition that day drive the next fiscal year's bill.

Proposition 2 1/2 caps the city's total levy, not each owner's bill. The levy can rise 2.5 percent over the prior year plus tax from new construction. One house can climb faster than that if its value rose faster than other homes, and the city's position is that taxes are fair as long as the assessed value is accurate.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to file an abatement

An abatement application is how you dispute a value or correct a billing error that made your tax too high. File it online, or send the paper form with your phone number, signature, date and supporting documents by email, fax or mail.

The process runs through the reason for the abatement, who may apply, the Assessor's action, a possible request for more information, payment of the tax, and an appeal to the Appellate Tax Board. Ask the Assessing Division what timing applies to the appeal step.

State law, M.G.L. c. 59, section 59, sets the filing deadline at the last day to pay the first actual installment without interest. Worcester's actual bills are issued January 1 and due 30 days later, so the window is short and opens near the end of January. Confirm the date with the office every year. Who can apply:

  • The person taxed, or the personal representative of that person's estate.
  • A tenant who pays rent and is bound to pay more than half the taxes.
  • Someone who gets title after January 1, who is treated as a taxpayer for this purpose.
  • A mortgage holder who has paid at least half the tax, during the last 10 days of the abatement period.

Exemptions

Worcester applies the state's statutory exemptions: persons over 70 who meet asset and income limits, surviving spouses with asset limits, blind persons, and owners with service-related disabilities. Qualifying owners must own the property in whole or in part and apply every year.

Applications for many of these can be filed by April 1 or within three months after the bill was sent, whichever is later. Churches, hospitals, schools and cultural groups may qualify under M.G.L. c. 59, section 5, but buying property does not make a religious or charitable group exempt on its own. It has to meet the criteria and file the right forms, which the city posts on its real estate tax page.

Expense reports for rental buildings

The city asks owners of income-producing property to report typical expenses, since the Assessor needs rent data to value those buildings fairly. Separate forms cover apartments, commercial and industrial property, and mixed use.

The information is for the assessor's use and is not public record. Report typical expenses only. If you paid for a big repair such as a new roof, do not report the whole cost in one year. An owner thinking of selling a three-family should expect rent and expense data to matter to the assessment.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Winter and the sale of an older house

Worcester winters are hard on roofs, pipes and heating systems, and buyers and inspectors check for that. The city averages about 64 inches of snow a season and is prone to nor'easters. Older buildings raise roof and heating questions, and a cash buyer who takes the house as is can skip repair negotiations. The tax balance still has to be cleared at closing.

Taxes at closing

Ask the Assessing Division and the Collector's office for a current balance before you list or accept an offer. The city's real estate tax page links to answers on unpaid bills, interest, mortgage company payments and changing the bill to a new owner's name.

Because bills are due 30 days after issue, a mid-year sale usually leaves one bill outstanding. The January 1 owner stays the assessed owner for the fiscal year, so the buyer should receive the seller's bill in care of the new name until the next year.

  • Check which of the four bills for the fiscal year are paid.
  • Ask whether interest has been added to a late bill.
  • Find out if you hold a statutory exemption that the buyer will not get.
  • Ask about the fee and timing for a municipal lien certificate.

If you owe back taxes

Unpaid bills do not stop you from selling. The closing attorney or title company pays what is owed from your proceeds, and you receive the remainder. Gather your bills for the year, note which quarters you have paid, and bring them when you call. Talk to us if you want to sell as is without repairs, and we will go through the numbers with you.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When are Worcester property tax bills due?

Worcester issues bills on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1. Payment is due 30 days after each issue date.

What is the Worcester residential tax rate?

Posted rates are $13.28 per $1,000 for residential property and $29.06 per $1,000 for commercial property, with no fiscal year attached. Check your bill for the year and rate.

How do I apply for a Worcester tax abatement?

Use the online application on the city's real estate tax page, or send the paper form to the Assessing Division by email, fax or mail. The deadline follows state law, so confirm it at 508-799-1098.

Why did my Worcester tax bill go up in January?

The July and October bills are preliminary estimates. The January and April bills use your new assessment and rate, so any change from reassessment shows up in those two.

Does Proposition 2 1/2 cap my own tax increase?

No. It limits the total amount the city can raise, plus new construction growth. An individual bill can rise by more than 2.5 percent if your value rose faster than other properties.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Cambridge property tax?

Cambridge housing in brief

Cambridge sits in Middlesex County directly across the Charles River from Boston. The 2020 census counted 118,403 residents on about 7 square miles, so a Cambridge house usually has close neighbors, and each parcel is valued and taxed on its own record. The city runs under a council-manager form of government, and the assessing and finance offices that handle your tax bill report to the city manager.

Demand follows the universities and the biotech and research employers around Kendall Square, and the squares, such as Harvard, Central, Inman and Porter, work as neighborhood centers. Heating systems, roofs and windows get heavy use through cold winters, so buyers' inspectors look at them closely.

Rent control ended in Massachusetts in 1994, and Cambridge's version had been unusually strict. Landlord-sellers with long-held rentals may still find old records worth checking.

Who bills Cambridge property tax and when

Assessing values the property and the Finance Department bills and collects. Cambridge bills twice a year. For FY2027 the first-half bill was issued October 19, 2026 and is due November 18, 2026, and the FY2027 rates are $6.95 per $1,000 residential and $16.99 per $1,000 commercial and industrial. Call the Finance Department for the second-half due date.

If your FY2027 first-half bill includes a water and sewer lien, contact the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. That office also handles municipal lien certificates and online payments.

Tax detailCambridge figure
FY2027 residential rate$6.95 per $1,000
FY2027 commercial and industrial rate$16.99 per $1,000
First-half bill issuedOctober 19, 2026
First-half bill dueNovember 18, 2026
Abatement periodOctober 19 to November 18, 2026
Residential exemption applicationApril 1, 2027
Assessing phone617-349-4343
Finance phone617-349-4220

How do I apply for the residential exemption?

The deadline is April 1 of the fiscal year, which for FY2027 means April 1, 2027. The exemption removes part of the value of an owner-occupied home from taxation, and Cambridge uses January 1 to test ownership and occupancy. For FY2027 the test date is January 1, 2026.

New owners should read this carefully. If you bought a Cambridge property and the exemption carried over from the previous owner, you must qualify on your own to keep it into the next fiscal year. Apply through the city's online portal, which requires a Viewpoint account, or ask Assessing for a paper form at 617-349-4343.

  • Other personal exemptions can be combined with it, but taxable value cannot fall below 10 percent of assessed value.
  • Income-related exemptions need a copy of the 2025 income tax return.
  • Assessing's office is at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, open Monday 8:30 to 8, Tuesday to Thursday 8:30 to 5, and Friday 8:30 to noon.

When you sell, the buyer is the one who needs to qualify. Do not tell a buyer the exemption will transfer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Abatement: how it works and how urgent it is

The FY2027 abatement window runs from October 19 to November 18, 2026, the same date the first-half bill is due. Assessed values follow full and fair cash value, meaning 100 percent of fair market value, reached through cost, income and market approaches.

To dispute a value, file with Assessing by mail or in person and be ready to show recent comparable sales. Assessing held online help sessions during the abatement period, and staff can be reached at 617-349-4343 or assessors@cambridgema.gov. If the result is not what you want, the next level is the Appellate Tax Board, and the clock there is three months from the decision.

Ask Assessing how a pending request affects the bill you owe before you hold back any payment.

What closing a Cambridge sale involves

The state steps apply here as they do everywhere in Massachusetts. A real estate attorney is customary and expected, and the state's deeds excise is $2.28 for every $500 of the sales price. Deeds are recorded at the Registry of Deeds, and masslandrecords.com lets you search the state's land records yourself before you list.

A seller also needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet the sale requirements, and the fire department charges a fee. Ask the Finance Department for a municipal lien certificate so you know exactly what is owed on the tax and any water or sewer lien before you set a closing date.

Income-based exemptions and records to pull

Beyond the residential exemption, Assessing handles personal exemptions that depend on age, income or other circumstances. Income-related ones need a copy of the 2025 income tax return, so owners who plan to apply should find that return before they call.

If you are selling, you will not be filing for the next fiscal year yourself, but the records still help. They show the buyer, the attorney and the lender what the house has been paying and why. Gather the last bill, the receipt for each payment and any letter Assessing sent after an abatement request.

Visit Assessing at 795 Massachusetts Avenue, Ground Floor, if you prefer to ask in person, or write to assessors@cambridgema.gov. Staff can explain how a request in progress affects the bill you owe, which is worth knowing before you set a closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Water and sewer charges on the tax bill

Cambridge runs its own municipal water system, and unpaid water and sewer charges can end up as a lien on the tax bill. That is why the lien certificate matters at a sale: it shows the tax and any water or sewer lien in one document.

If your first-half bill shows such a lien, call the Finance Department at 617-349-4220 before closing. Your attorney will want the figure, and a buyer's lender will want it paid or escrowed at the table.

Preparing to sell, step by step

A Cambridge sale goes faster when the tax side is settled early.

  1. Pay or confirm the first-half bill, due November 18, 2026, and keep the receipt.
  2. Decide whether to file an abatement, since the window closes on that same date.
  3. Request a municipal lien certificate from the Finance Department.
  4. Order the smoke and carbon monoxide certificate from the local fire department.
  5. Tell your attorney whether you are receiving the residential exemption, so the buyer knows to apply on their own.

If the house needs work or has tenants, a cash buyer can close without the lender's repair list. The tax, lien and recording steps are the same for every buyer.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Cambridge residential property tax rate for FY2027?

The FY2027 residential rate is $6.95 per $1,000 of assessed value, and the commercial and industrial rate is $16.99 per $1,000.

When is the first-half Cambridge tax bill due?

The first-half FY2027 real estate bill was issued October 19, 2026 and is due November 18, 2026. Cambridge bills twice a year, so call the Finance Department for the second-half date.

What is the deadline for a Cambridge abatement in FY2027?

The abatement period runs October 19 to November 18, 2026. Contact the Assessing Department at 617-349-4343 right away if you plan to file.

Will the residential exemption transfer to the buyer of my Cambridge house?

No, the buyer has to qualify on their own. A new owner who inherited the exemption must still qualify to keep receiving it in the next fiscal year.

How do I find out what is owed before selling a Cambridge house?

Request a municipal lien certificate from the Finance Department at 617-349-4220. That office also handles online payments.

Somerville at a glance

Somerville is a Middlesex County city on Boston's northwest edge, next to Cambridge, Medford, Everett and Arlington. The 2020 count was 81,045 residents packed into roughly 4.2 square miles, the densest municipality in New England. Small lots and multifamily houses are the norm, and neighborhoods grew up around commercial squares such as Union, Davis, Ball, Magoun, Teele and Gilman. The Red Line reached Davis Square in 1984. Ask the Assessing Department how your parcel is classified and valued, since blocks near different squares can price very differently.

Who to call

Two offices share the work. Assessing sets values, keeps ownership and mailing records, and decides abatements. The Treasurer/Collector bills and collects.

  • Assessing: assessing@somervillema.gov or 617-625-6600, extension 3100.
  • Treasury: 93 Highland Avenue, Somerville, MA 02143, treasury@somervillema.gov, 617-625-6600, extension 3500.
  • Treasury hours: Monday to Wednesday 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Thursday 8:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m., Friday 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

Doxo has no affiliation with the city. Pay online only through somervillema.gov/Payments.

Due dates and bill types

Bills come quarterly and are payable August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, with the fiscal year running July 1 to June 30. When a date falls on a weekend or holiday, payment moves to the next business day. Each bill is mailed one month before it is due.

QuarterCoversDueType of bill
1July 1 to Sept. 30Aug. 1Preliminary (estimated)
2Oct. 1 to Dec. 31Nov. 1Preliminary (estimated)
3Jan. 1 to March 31Feb. 1Actual
4April 1 to June 30May 1Actual

The estimated bills use last year's actual tax plus 2.5%, split four ways. In December the assessors fix the real tax for the year, and the two estimated payments come off it. Call Assessing for the rate on your property class.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens if a payment is late?

Somerville ignores postmarks. A bill is paid only on the day the Treasurer receives it. After that, the charges stack up:

  • Real estate, personal property and water balances accrue 14% interest under M.G.L. c. 59, sections 57 and 57C.
  • Once the city takes the tax, tax title interest is 16% under M.G.L. c. 60, section 62.
  • A returned check costs $25, plus 1% if it exceeds $2,500.
  • A fourth quarter bill paid late gets an $18 demand fee.
  • Unpaid water, sewer or ticket liens are moved onto the third quarter bill.

Never receiving a bill is not an excuse. One is generated for every parcel, and the owner must ask for a duplicate when it does not arrive. The Treasurer/Collector's page also links delinquent real estate information and a tax title report.

How to appeal your assessment

The abatement application must reach the Assessors by February 1, 2027 at 4:30 p.m. A late filing means the Board of Assessors can no longer abate the bill.

  1. Get the form at the Assessor's Office or download it from the city's abatement page.
  2. Deliver it by hand, mail it with a postmark of February 1 or earlier, or send it by fax or to assessing@somervillema.gov, as long as it arrives by close of business that day.
  3. The Board of Assessors has three months from the application date to rule.
  4. If you disagree, appeal to the state Appellate Tax Board within three months of the Board's notice.

Filing does not pause collection, so keep paying on time. That avoids interest and protects your appeal rights.

Taxes after you sell

Whoever owns the property on January 1 appears on the bills for that fiscal year, so one can arrive after you have moved out. A buyer can ask Assessing to add a c/o line with the new name. At closing, confirm that your mortgage company and your attorney do not both pay the same installment.

Refunds follow the same rule. A credit on a real estate or personal property bill goes at year end to the January 1 record owner and does not carry into the next year. If a transfer happens mid-year, settle it at closing.

  • Order a municipal lien certificate. Fees are $80 for a single family, condo, two family or three family, $250 for four to eight units, and $350 for more than eight.
  • Get a final water reading from the Water Department and hand it to closing counsel so any credit is received at closing. A water credit from overestimated bills that will not be used within the next billing cycle needs a written refund request to Water and Sewer at 17 Franey Road.
  • In a newly developed condominium building the master parcel may still carry a single tax bill, and the association must keep that account at zero on each due date.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can I sell if I owe tax?

Yes. The lien certificate shows what is owed, and the balance is paid from sale proceeds at closing. A cash buyer can purchase the house as is with the bill outstanding, and the title company settles the amount before funds reach you.

If a bill stays unpaid, the city can take the tax and publish a notice of tax taking, and the balance then runs at the 16% tax title rate. That is a good reason to act early. Call or text us with your address and the amount you think you owe, and we will tell you what we can offer, with no obligation.

Timing a sale around the billing cycle

Because the first two bills are estimates and the last two are actual, the amount due at closing can change depending on the month. A sale before the third quarter still has actual bills ahead, and those reflect the new assessment. Ask closing counsel how the year will be prorated between you and the buyer, and compare that with the bills you have in hand.

If a bill is due within days of the closing date, pay it yourself or have the attorney confirm it in writing. Because Somerville credits only payments it has received, a payment still in the mail on the due date counts as late. Keep the receipt or confirmation number for every payment so you can show it at the table if a question comes up.

Steps to a sale when you are behind

  1. Order the municipal lien certificate so you know the exact balance, including any water, sewer or ticket liens.
  2. Ask Treasury whether the account has moved to tax title, since the interest rate changes from 14% to 16%.
  3. Gather the final water reading and any refund requests.
  4. Give your closing attorney or title company the certificate so they can pay the city from proceeds.
  5. After closing, forward any bill that still carries your name to the buyer, who can ask Assessing for a c/o line.

A cash sale follows the same steps, just without waiting for a lender.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

When are Somerville property taxes due?

Payments are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30, and bills are mailed one month ahead.

What is the deadline to file a Somerville abatement?

February 1, 2027 at 4:30 p.m. Mailed applications need a postmark of February 1 or earlier, and fax or email filings must arrive by close of business.

Does Somerville accept postmarks for tax payments?

No. A bill counts as paid only when the Treasurer receives the payment, whatever the postmark says.

What interest does Somerville charge on late property tax?

Late real estate, personal property and water balances carry 14%. Once a tax is taken and moved to tax title, the rate is 16%.

I sold my house but still got a tax bill. What now?

The January 1 owner's name stays on the bill for that fiscal year. Confirm your attorney handled the proration, then pass the bill to the new owner, who can ask Assessing to add a c/o line.

Quincy, MA Property Tax Guide: Offices, Dates and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in Massachusetts

Quincy in brief

Quincy, in Norfolk County just south of Boston, counted 101,636 residents in 2020 and 51,156 housing units. Commuters like the four Red Line stops (North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams) plus Interstate 93 and Route 3.

Neighborhoods vary a lot. Squantum, Houghs Neck and Adams Shore are coastal and mostly peninsular, and began as summer communities before turning into year-round homes. Wollaston and North Quincy are dense and sit on the Red Line. Quincy Center holds City Hall and the historic core. Buyers eyeing an older waterside house tend to question the furnace, roof and basement.

Who bills and who assesses

Quincy divides the job. One office decides value, and the other collects.

The Assessors' Office sets values on roughly 27,000 parcels of every type, from homes to utilities. Abatement and exemption requests land on its desk. It stands behind its values when they are challenged at the state tax appeals board, and every sale in the city gets reported by it to the state revenue department. Visit 1305 Hancock Street, 1st Floor, or call (617) 376-1170, weekdays 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

Each year's rate grows out of a budget the Mayor and City Council set. A classification hearing in the Council Chamber comes first, then the council votes the rates, and the Assessors hand the total to the Treasurer-Collector. A disputed bill means two separate calls: the Assessors for value, the collector for payment.

Due dates and installments

Four installments fall due each fiscal year: August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.

Bills one and two are estimates. Added together they come to about half of last year's tax, divided into two equal payments. Bills three and four use the new assessed value and new rate and credit what you paid. Your new value first appears on the third bill, mailed in January.

BillDue dateWhat it reflects
Quarter 1August 1Preliminary, half of the prior-year total split in two
Quarter 2November 1Preliminary, second half of that amount
Quarter 3February 1Actual bill with new value and rate
Quarter 4May 1Final installment of the actual bill

Timing affects a sale. A house listed in early spring has three of the year's bills in play, and the payoff at closing depends on which have been paid.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Tax rate

Quincy's residential rate for fiscal year 2026 is $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000. The city's tax rates page keeps the history:

  • Fiscal 2024: $11.27 residential, $22.45 commercial
  • Fiscal 2025: $11.53 residential, $23.01 commercial
  • Fiscal 2026: $11.78 residential, $23.53 commercial

For a rough estimate, multiply assessed value by the rate, divide by 1,000 and subtract any exemption. The bill itself is what counts.

How to appeal your assessment

An appeal begins with an abatement application to the Assessors. The usual deadline in a quarterly-billing city is February 1.

The Massachusetts Appellate Tax Board explains each step in its guide to real estate tax appeals. Here is the sequence.

  • Keep paying on schedule. Paying on time is a jurisdictional requirement, with narrow exceptions such as a tax of $5,000 or less.
  • Submit the approved abatement form by the date the actual bill's first installment is due.
  • The Assessors get three months. Inaction for three calendar months is treated as a denial.
  • Still unhappy? You have three months from their decision, or from the deemed denial, to file at the Appellate Tax Board.

The board starts by presuming the assessment is right, so you must show the fair cash value is lower. Comparable recent sales nearby, in similar condition, do that best. A tax increase on its own proves nothing.

Exemptions

Several groups qualify for statutory exemptions in Quincy, and you reapply each year. For fiscal year 2027 the filing deadline is April 1, 2027.

  • Senior citizens, with separate applications for ages 65 and up and ages 70 and up
  • Legally blind residents
  • Surviving spouses, and minor children of a deceased parent
  • Surviving spouses or minor children of police officers and firefighters
  • Disabled former service members, including anyone with a service-related disability of at least 10 percent

At minimum, you must be domiciled in Quincy. The Assessors also publish a tax deferral explanation for owners who qualify. Forms and details are on the exemption programs page.

Selling after a health change or a death in the family? Ask the Assessors whether an exemption you hold alters the final bill and the payoff.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

If Quincy property tax goes unpaid

A lien attaches automatically when property tax goes unpaid. In time the city may record a taking, and a private holder may pursue foreclosure in Land Court. The court's foreclosure overview shows the usual path.

  1. After 30 days of nonpayment on a tax or water and sewer bill, a demand can be mailed to your last known address.
  2. If 14 more days pass without payment, a tax taking can be recorded at the Registry of Deeds.
  3. The tax title may end up with a private party, for instance after a bundled sale or an auction.
  4. Six or twelve months after the taking or sale, depending on the date, the holder may file a Land Court complaint.
  5. You may respond, request a hearing, and redeem by paying all taxes, interest and fees before a final judgment of foreclosure.

You can redeem right up until the court enters judgment. Many owners in arrears sell for that reason: the closing pays off the lien, and any equity left is yours.

Closing costs and paperwork

A Quincy sale brings a deed excise tax, a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate, and payoff of any tax owed.

  • The Norfolk County Registry of Deeds charges a deed excise tax of $2.28 per $500 of the stated consideration. Its fee schedule also lists a $156 recording fee for a deed in recorded land.
  • A one or two family home needs a certificate of compliance from the local fire department showing that smoke and carbon monoxide alarms meet state requirements. The state's guidance says to call the fire department as soon as you have a closing date.
  • Ask both the Assessors and the Treasurer-Collector for the current balance, because the closing agent needs an exact payoff.
  • Bring your deed information and latest bill when you call, so the offices can find the parcel quickly.

A cash sale to Cash Home Buyers still needs these same items, but it skips the lender appraisal and the repair negotiations that often follow one. We buy houses as-is, so the alarm certificate is the main inspection task left, and the tax payoff is handled through closing.

Frequently asked questions

How often is Quincy property tax billed?

Quarterly, due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. The first two bills are preliminary and total about half of the prior year's tax.

What is Quincy's residential tax rate?

For fiscal year 2026 it is $11.78 per $1,000 of assessed value. The commercial rate is $23.53 per $1,000.

Can I sell my Quincy house if I owe back property tax?

Yes. Unpaid tax is a lien on the property, and the sale can pay it from the proceeds at closing. Get a written payoff figure from the city before the closing date.

What is the deadline for a Quincy property tax exemption?

Applications for fiscal year 2027 are due on or before April 1, 2027, and you must file again every year. You must be domiciled in Quincy.

How long do I have to challenge my Quincy assessment?

The abatement application is generally due February 1. After the Assessors act, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Waltham property tax offices

Waltham sits in Middlesex County about 9 miles west of Downtown Boston. Bentley, Brandeis, a deep employer base and commuter rail at Central Square keep homes in demand, and serious buyers ask about the tax bill early. Two City Hall offices split the work.

  • Assessors Office (City Hall, 25 Lexington Street, 781-314-3200): decides what each parcel is worth and takes abatement, exemption and tax relief paperwork.
  • Treasurer/Collector (610 Main Street, 781-314-3250, Monday to Friday, 8:30 am to 4:30 pm): sends bills, takes payments, and handles tax title and municipal lien certificates.

Call the Assessors when your question is about how much the bill is. Call the Collector when it is about where to pay or what you owe today.

Due dates and penalties

Waltham sends a real estate bill every quarter, payable August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1, and the city's fiscal year begins July 1. When one of those dates is a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, you have until the next business day.

QuarterDue dateType of bill
FirstAugust 1Preliminary, based on last year's tax
SecondNovember 1Preliminary, based on last year's tax
ThirdFebruary 1Actual, based on this year's assessment and rate
FourthMay 1Actual, based on this year's assessment and rate

Payment is credited on the day the Collector's office receives it. No bill in the mail 30 days ahead of a due date? Phone the office and ask for a copy. Late balances accrue 14 percent a year in interest.

Why the third and fourth bills run higher

Quarters one and two are placeholders worth about half of last year's tax, calculated before the new value and rate exist. Quarters three and four settle the account. The city works out your real tax for the year, credits your first two payments, and divides the difference between the last two bills.

That is where a higher value, a changed rate or a betterment charge shows up. Three situations make the jump larger than owners expect:

  • Your assessment rose faster than the city's overall levy.
  • Betterments, special assessments or interest were added during the year.
  • The house changed hands, and the earlier owner's personal exemption did not transfer to the buyer.

For a seller, this timing matters at closing. An August payment can still be followed by a bigger balance in February.

Whose name is on the bill after a sale?

Waltham fixes value and ownership on January 1. Whoever owned the house that day is named on all four bills for the fiscal year, and a later buyer receives them addressed to the seller, care of the new owner.

The buyer's own name appears as assessed owner beginning with the next fiscal year. The Assessors Office wants to hear from new owners, but it cannot swap the name until the new deed comes over from the Registry of Deeds. Until then it puts the buyer on the mailing line.

The buyer has a safeguard in M.G.L. c. 59, section 59: a person who takes title after January 1 is treated as a taxpayer when it comes to abatements, so the new owner may contest a bill printed with your name.

Residential exemption

An owner-occupied home gets a reduction in assessed value through the residential exemption, which Waltham set at $317,643 for fiscal year 2026. Principal residences with up to three units are eligible.

  • You are the owner on January 1.
  • It is your principal residence, the same address you use for income tax.
  • If a trust holds the home, you file a copy of the trust with the Assessors for review.

Owners not already receiving it can apply until April 1 each year. The exemption appears on the third quarter actual bill, and an approved late application is credited to the fourth quarter bill or refunded if the tax is already paid in full.

Rental or vacant houses get nothing, so an investor who buys yours may pay a higher bill than you did.

How to challenge your assessment

Abatement applications go to the Assessors Office. The statute, M.G.L. c. 59, section 59, sets the cutoff at the last day you can pay the first actual installment interest-free. Here that installment is the third quarter bill due February 1, so aim for that date and check it with the Assessors.

The city posts a state form for abatements, Form 128. The assessors say they value a home as a buyer would, weighing location, interior condition, size, and kitchen and bath quality, then comparing nearby sales. They want applicants to give a specific reason for the complaint. Useful evidence includes:

  • Mistakes on the property record card, such as the wrong square footage or number of baths.
  • Nearby homes similar to yours that recently sold below your assessed value.
  • Photos or repair estimates showing a condition the assessment missed.

A tenant whose lease makes them responsible for over half the taxes may also file. Mailed filings count on the date of the United States postmark.

Tax relief for older or disabled owners

Low-income elderly and low-income disabled residents can turn to the Tax Relief Program run by the Taxation Fund Committee. It covers a share of the real estate tax for applicants who meet its guidelines, with preference for the greatest need.

Applications are accepted each year from July 1 to November 5. Get the form from the Assessors Office, City Hall, 25 Lexington Street, 781-314-3200. Donations that residents check off on the envelope sent with the tax bill support the fund. The Collector's office also runs a Senior Work Off Program.

Before you close on a Waltham house

Request two things from the Treasurer/Collector: today's balance and a municipal lien certificate. The same office issues the certificate and runs tax title, and the document shows every amount owed on the property. For the current rate, check your latest bill or call the Assessors.

  • Gather the last four quarterly bills and mark the paid ones.
  • Ask whether the Collector has added interest.
  • Tell the Assessors if you recently bought, so future bills carry your name.

Selling with taxes owed

You can sell with taxes unpaid. At closing the title company or your attorney settles the balance out of the proceeds and sends you the rest. Get the lien certificate first so every party works from one figure. A cash buyer will take the house as is with a bill still open, so you do not have to scramble to pay a quarter or two beforehand.

Interest keeps building on an overdue balance, so waiting costs more. Send us the address by call or text and we will tell you what we can offer, with no obligation.

Frequently asked questions

When are Waltham property taxes due?

The four payment dates are August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. A weekend date rolls to Monday or the next business day.

How much interest does Waltham charge on late real estate tax?

The rate is 14 percent a year on unpaid bills. Call the Collector at 781-314-3250 to learn the exact figure on your account.

Can I get a Waltham tax abatement if I just bought the house?

Yes. A person who acquires title after January 1 is treated as a taxpayer for abatements under the state statute. File with the Assessors Office and confirm the deadline there.

Why does my Waltham bill still show the old owner?

The January 1 owner is named for the whole fiscal year. Later buyers get bills in care of the new owner, and their own name starts the next fiscal year.

Who do I call about a Waltham tax lien certificate?

Phone the Treasurer/Collector at 781-314-3250. Ask what it costs, how many days it takes and whether the request must be in writing.

Newton at a glance

Sitting in Middlesex County roughly 8 miles from downtown Boston, Newton has no single center. Thirteen villages make up the city: Auburndale, Chestnut Hill, Newton Centre, Newton Corner, Newton Highlands, Newton Lower Falls, Newton Upper Falls, Newtonville, Nonantum, Oak Hill, Thompsonville, Waban and West Newton.

Your village shapes your ZIP code, your commute and the kind of house on your street, and leaves the billing office the same. Billing belongs to the city's Assessing and Treasury offices. Because streetcar lines, the railroad and later the car brought building in waves, the housing stock is mixed in age, and older houses often come with aging roofs and heating systems that buyers ask about.

Demand stays steady. Colleges, a hospital, the MBTA Green Line, the Worcester commuter rail, the Massachusetts Turnpike and Route 9 all keep buyers interested in Newton houses.

Who bills, who assesses

Two city offices share the job. Assessing decides what your property is worth and takes abatement and exemption requests. Treasury sends the bills and takes the money.

OfficeWhat it handlesHow to reach it
AssessingValues, abatements, exemptions, tax mailing addressCity Hall, Room 111, 1000 Commonwealth Avenue, Newton Centre, MA 02459. 617-796-1160, assessing@newtonma.gov. Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
TreasuryPayments, balances, duplicate bills, refunds, municipal lien certificates, tax title617-796-1330, treasury@newtonma.gov

Pick the right door. A jump in your value is a question for Assessing. A payment that may not have posted is a question for Treasury.

Current tax rate

The fiscal year 2026 rate is certified at $9.69 for every $1,000 of assessed value on residential property, and $18.06 on commercial, industrial and personal property. Exemptions or abatements can bring your own bill below the plain rate.

  • The rate is reset every fiscal year, so next year's bill will use a different figure.
  • Because the rate is applied to your assessed value, a lower value from an abatement lowers the bill.
  • The city's Assessor's Database and map lets you look up your parcel and see its assessed value.
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When is Newton property tax due?

Newton bills in four installments. Each falls on the first business day of the month in August, November, February and May.

  • August 1 and November 1 cover the first half of the fiscal year.
  • February 1 and May 1 cover the second half.
  • Excise bills on vehicles come due 30 days after issue, and quarterly utility bills give you 30 days from the bill date.

That first installment date doubles as your abatement deadline. The application has to reach the assessors by the day the first installment of the actual bill comes due, which is generally February 1 where billing is quarterly. Your bill prints the exact dates.

Appealing your assessment

A value you believe is too high can be contested through an abatement application at Newton's Assessing office. Two habits protect your case: file before the deadline, and keep paying while you wait. The state's Appellate Tax Board guide names three musts: payment by each due date, an abatement form filed on time, and any later appeal to the Board filed on time.

Assessors then get three months to answer. If they never do, the application is treated as denied when three calendar months run out. Either way, a further three months starts, and that is your window to go to the Appellate Tax Board.

Expect to carry the proof. An assessment starts out presumed valid, and it reflects the value on January 1 before the fiscal year begins, so a fiscal year 2025 bill reflects January 1, 2024. Recent sales of comparable homes nearby make the strongest evidence.

  • Pay every installment by its due date, even with an abatement pending.
  • File the form with Assessing ahead of the deadline on your bill.
  • Gather photos, the property record card and comparable sales.
  • Write down the dates you filed and any reply, so the three-month clock is easy to track.

A few narrow exceptions to the payment rule exist, so read the guide before you decide to skip a payment.

Checking your own bill

Before you decide to appeal or sell, read your bill from top to bottom. It lists your assessed value, the installment dates and what has been paid. Compare the value to what similar houses in your village have sold for. If the gap is large, an abatement may be worth the paperwork. If it is small, the time is better spent on the sale.

Duplicate bills and refunds also come from Treasury. If you never received a bill, or you paid and the balance still shows, call 617-796-1330 before the next installment date. Unpaid quarters can turn into a larger problem at closing, and a quick call now is easier than a payoff scramble later.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Exemptions and tax assistance

Newton offers exemption, deferral, work-off and assistance programs for eligible taxpayers. FY2027 applications are available now, and exemption applications are due by April 1, 2027. Plan around an April 1 cutoff in later years too.

Call Assessing to learn which program fits your age, income or status. Homeowners who are about to sell should ask whether an exemption or deferral changes the payoff at closing, then let the closing attorney request the figure.

Preparing to sell

Some groundwork with the two city offices saves time later. Collect these items.

  • Your latest tax bill, with its installment dates and any quarter still unpaid.
  • The property record card in the Assessor's Database, which shows how the city describes the house.
  • Any exemption or deferral paperwork, in case it changes the closing payoff.
  • Notes on any open abatement, including the date you filed.

Timing matters too. Selling partway through a fiscal year means the year's tax is divided between you and the buyer, and the closing attorney works that out on the settlement statement. Ask early so nothing surprises you at the table.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and mortgage approval, two steps that can slow a sale of an older house. The tax work above still applies, but fewer parties are involved.

Selling with taxes owed

For any balance, start with Treasury before you sell. It handles municipal lien certificate requests and can explain tax title, redemptions and municipal lien releases.

  1. Ask Treasury what you owe, including any quarter still open.
  2. Request the municipal lien certificate through Treasury so the buyer's side can see the balance.
  3. Ask Assessing for your current assessment and whether an abatement is open.
  4. Tell your closing attorney how the balance should be paid. It is normally settled out of the sale proceeds.

A badly overdue account calls for an early talk with Treasury about tax title and redemption. Waiting only gives a buyer's lawyer more to untangle.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Newton houses in as-is condition, with no repairs and no listing. Want an offer on a house that still has taxes due? Reach out, and the payoff gets handled through closing.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the Newton tax bill?

Treasury sends the bill and collects payment. Assessing sets the value. The Treasury number is 617-796-1330.

When are Newton property taxes due?

Four times a year, on the first business day of August, November, February and May. Your bill lists each date.

Newton's residential rate?

Certified for FY2026 at $9.69 per $1,000 of value for homes. Commercial, industrial and personal property is $18.06.

When must I file an abatement?

By the first installment due date on the bill, generally February 1 where billing is quarterly. Call Assessing at 617-796-1160 to confirm your date.

Can I sell with unpaid Newton tax?

Yes. Your closing attorney arranges the payoff, and Treasury issues municipal lien certificates and can tell you the balance.

Owe Springfield Property Tax? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Springfield property tax?
We buy Springfield houses as-is, and the title company pays unpaid tax from the proceeds.
Get My Cash Offer →

Springfield and its tax offices

Springfield is the seat of Hampden County, on the east bank of the Connecticut River in western Massachusetts. The 2020 census counted 155,929 residents, the third most in the state. Housing runs from the Victorian Painted Ladies of McKnight and Forest Park Heights to postwar suburban streets in Sixteen Acres and old mill housing in Indian Orchard, so assessed values vary a lot from one neighborhood to the next.

The city's Division of Finance runs property tax. You will deal with two offices: the Assessors Office at 36 Court Street, which sets values, and the Collector/Treasurer, which bills and collects.

Storm damage and repair records

A tornado with winds above 160 miles per hour hit Springfield on June 1, 2011. It killed three people and left more than 500 homeless, and the South End was among the neighborhoods struck. If your house was damaged then or in a later storm, gather the repair records and permits and tell us about them when you ask for an offer. Buyers care less about the storm than about whether the work was done and documented.

Assessors and Collector/Treasurer

The Assessors Office is at Room 09, 36 Court Street, Springfield, MA 01103, and takes signed faxes at 413-787-7721. Call 311, or 413-736-3111 from outside the city, for help.

  • The Collector prepares bills, collects real estate, personal property and excise taxes, trash fees and parking fines, and handles tax-taking of delinquent properties.
  • The Treasurer holds properties foreclosed for taxes, handles redemption payments and maintenance, and runs the auctions of those properties.

The city's site lets you view real estate bills and payment history back to 2004. It also has a tax repayment agreement form and a municipal lien certificate request form.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

When are bills mailed and due?

Springfield bills quarterly, and each bill goes out 30 days before its due date.

QuarterBill issuedPayment due
1July 1August 1
2October 1November 1
3January 1February 1
4April 1May 1

Values are set as of January 1. Most homes are valued by comparing the prior year's sales. Income property may be valued by income, and special-purpose buildings by replacement cost less depreciation. Residential, commercial and personal property each get their own rate.

No bill in the mail does not cancel the debt. You still owe the tax and any interest, so request a duplicate through 311 and allow ten business days. Have the street and parcel code ready to speed it up.

How to file an abatement

Applications go to the Assessors Office by February 1, and only after the third quarter bill has been issued. You cannot file for earlier years, and a late filing cannot be granted.

  1. Pick up the form at the Assessors Office. Do not send it in with a tax payment.
  2. Choose your ground: overvaluation, disproportionate assessment, improper classification or a statutory exemption.
  3. Deliver it to Room 09 at 36 Court Street, mail it postmarked by the deadline, or fax it.
  4. Wait up to 90 days. The Assessors must rule within that time and tell you in writing.
  5. To appeal, file with the Appellate Tax Board at 100 Cambridge Street, Boston within three months of the decision. Filing fees may apply.

The Assessors may ask for information or access to inspect the house, and refusing can cost you the appeal. Keep paying meanwhile, because filing does not delay collection.

How the city sets your value

Each parcel is valued as of January 1, and the Assessors treat every property on its own. Two houses a few blocks apart can carry quite different bills even though both are in Springfield. For an ordinary house the method is the market approach: sales from the year before are compared with your property and adjusted for differences. Rental buildings may be valued from their income, and special-purpose buildings from replacement cost less depreciation.

Because classes get separate rates, it helps to confirm how your parcel is classified. Improper classification is one of the listed grounds for an abatement, so check the class printed on your bill and ask the Assessors if it looks wrong.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Paying and getting help

The city site shows bills and payment history, so start there before you call. If you are behind, the tax repayment agreement form on the same site is worth a look, since an agreement with the Collector may be a better route than waiting for collection action. Bring your parcel code, the street address and any notices you have received when you phone 311 or visit Room 09 at 36 Court Street.

Remember that trash fees and parking fines are collected through the same office and can appear alongside your tax. A clean lien certificate needs those cleared as well, so ask for the full list of what is open.

Why the old owner's name stays on the bill

Springfield fixes ownership as of January 1 and keeps that name on the bill through the fiscal year, which ends in June. After a mid-year sale the paperwork can look wrong even when everything is correct. The bill is not a claim that you still own the house. It is simply addressed to the record owner on that date. Forward it to the buyer without changing it, and keep a copy of the closing statement showing how the tax was split. If a question comes up later, that statement and the lien certificate are the documents that settle it.

Selling with taxes owed

Once the sale is final, the buyer is responsible for the tax, and your share is normally deducted from the price at closing. The bill still carries the January 1 owner's name until the new fiscal year starts July 1, so forward it to the buyer unchanged.

  • Each side's lawyer should get a municipal lien certificate from the Collector before closing.
  • Unpaid taxes can lead to collection action, up to foreclosure.
  • Trash fees and parking tickets are separate bills in the same system, so check them as well.

We buy Springfield houses as is, including those with tax arrears. The title company pays what is owed from the proceeds and you keep the remainder. If you are behind, ask the Collector about a repayment agreement before you decide.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Steps when a sale is close

  1. Ask the Collector for the lien certificate and read every line, including trash fees and parking tickets.
  2. Look at your bills for the current fiscal year and see which quarters remain.
  3. Give the certificate to the title company or attorney so they can plan the payoff.
  4. After closing, forward any bill with your name on it to the buyer.

A cash sale follows these same steps without waiting on a lender, so you can often pick a closing date that suits you.

Frequently asked questions

When are Springfield property taxes due?

Payments are due August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1. Bills are issued 30 days earlier, on July 1, October 1, January 1 and April 1.

Where do I file a Springfield abatement application?

Take it to the Assessors Office, Room 09, 36 Court Street, or fax a signed copy to 413-787-7721. It must be filed by February 1 and is available only after the third quarter bill is issued.

How long do the Springfield Assessors have to decide?

They have 90 days from the date you file. If you disagree, you have three months to appeal to the Appellate Tax Board.

Who owes tax if I sell after January 1?

The bill carries the January 1 owner's name, but the new owner is responsible once the sale closes. The seller's share is usually deducted from the price at closing.

How do I get a duplicate Springfield tax bill?

Contact Springfield 311 online or call 311, or 413-736-3111 from outside the city. Allow ten business days and have the street and parcel code ready.
